cues.text: Three Centuries of Persecution

From Nero 's reign in the first century through the 'Great Persecution' launched by Diocletian in 303, Christians in the Roman Empire faced recurring waves of imprisonment, confiscation, and execution.
Even the earlier Edict of Serdica, issued by the dying Galerius in 311, only conceded that the persecutions had failed to eradicate the faith — it granted a grudging toleration, not true freedom.

By the early fourth century the Church had nonetheless grown into a substantial and organized presence across the Empire, from Britain to Mesopotamia, held together by bishops, creeds, and an unbroken memory of its martyrs.
The Meeting at Milan
In early 313, the Western emperor Constantine , fresh from victory over Maxentius at the Milvian Bridge, met his Eastern counterpart Licinius .
They met at Mediolanum (modern Milan ) to cement their alliance, sealed by Licinius's marriage to Constantine's sister.
Among the political business settled there was a joint religious policy, later circulated as an imperial letter to provincial governors throughout the East.
The text does not survive as a single formal 'edict' in the technical sense.
It is preserved through the writings of the Christian author Lactantius and the historian Eusebius of Caesarea.
They each transmit versions of the letter sent out in Constantine and Licinius's names.
Terms of the Toleration
The letter declared that no one , Christian or otherwise, should be denied the freedom to follow the religion of his choosing.

It restored to Christian communities, without cost, churches and properties that had been confiscated during the persecutions, and it extended the same liberty of worship to every religion in the Empire, not Christianity alone.
As one contemporary rendering of the text put it: “no man whatever should be refused complete toleration.”
This applied to anyone who had given up his mind either to the cult of the Christians or to the religion he personally felt best suited to himself.
Constantine's Path to Christian Favor
Constantine had attributed his victory at the Milvian Bridge in 312 to the God of the Christians, after a reported vision of a heavenly sign before the battle.

Milan did not make Christianity the state religion — that step waited until the Edict of Thessalonica in 380 — but it ended the era in which practicing the faith could cost a Christian his property, freedom, or life.

In the years that followed, Constantine went further than mere toleration: he funded church building, returned clergy exemptions from civic burdens once granted to pagan priests, and personally convened the Council of Nicaea in 325 to settle the Arian controversy.
Legacy
The Edict of Milan is remembered as the hinge between the Age of Martyrs and the era of an openly public Church.
It allowed Christian communities to organize visibly, build basilicas, and hold councils — conditions without which the Church's rapid growth across the fourth century would have been unthinkable.
Modern commemorations have continued to mark 313 as a foundational date for religious liberty in the West.
These include a major 1,700th-anniversary observance in 2013, even as historians debate how much genuine 'toleration' — as opposed to eventual establishment — Constantine himself intended.
